newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge say support ousted prince.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge say support ousted prince.

text.p: The Khmer Rouge guerrillas, who recently purged their notorious leader Pol Pot, said on Thursday they supported Cambodia's ousted co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

The guerrilla group sealed an agreement with the prince's royalist party on July 4, the day before fighting erupted in Phnom Penh leading to Ranariddh's ouster by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, the Far Eastern Economic Review reported on Thursday.

A new generation of younger Khmer Rouge leaders wanted to join forces with the royalists and others and Pol Pot was purged for his violent opposition to the move, the magazine's correspondent, Nate Thayer, reported.
But Cambodian strongman Hun Sen said Pol Pot's purge and trial was "a political farce" and he proposed measures to arrest the shadowy figure and bring him before an international tribunal.

Khmer Rouge front man Khieu Samphan, one of the main leaders of the rebel faction which broke with Pol Pot, said his political party, the National Solidarity Party, would join all other groups in opposing Hun Sen.
"We still recognise Prince Norodom Ranariddh as the legal first prime minister of the country," Khieu Samphan said in a guerrilla radio broadcast monitored in Phnom Penh.

"We oppose any nomination to replace Prince Norodom Ranariddh," he said, referring to Foreign Minister Ung Huot whose nomination for the prince's job is backed by Hun Sen and is due to be approved by the Cambodian parliament within days.
Ranariddh has denied any links with the Khmer Rouge but a senior royalist commander spoke recently of the possibility of striking a military alliance with the guerrillas.
Khmer Rouge radio has launched regular attacks on Hun Sen since the prince's July 5-6 ouster, deriding him as a "puppet" of Vietnam and calling for oppostion to his rule.
"The National Solidarity Party joins and supports all national forces and all political parties who implement policies to oppose and destroy ... the puppet Hun Sen," Khieu Samphan said on Thursday.
The royalists and the Khmer Rouge were battlefield allies during the 1980s when they fought a Vietnamese army of occupation and Hun Sen's Hanoi-backed government.
Pol Pot, under whose 1975-79 "killing fields" rule more than one million Cambodians died, was condemned by his former comrades and sentenced to life under house arrest at a show trial last Friday.

The Khmer Rouge are seeking to build alliances both in the country and overseas for their fight against Hun Sen's government and "Vietnamese aggressors", the Hong Kong-based Far Eastern Economic Review reported.
"The reason we put an end to the Pol Pot regime is because we want the international community to see and help us in our struggle," a senior Khmer Rouge officer told the magazine.
Hun Sen said this week that Pol Pot still led the Khmer Rouge and his trial was a game.

In an interview with ABC-TV's "Nightline" programme, Hun Sen said his two-stage plan called for the Cambodian government to gain control of the Anlong Veng area, the rebels' main headquarters, through Khmer Rouge defections and "military measures".
U.S. government officials have been quoted as saying that Hun Sen could rehabilitate his reputation by turning Pol Pot over.
Since Hun Sen's ouster of his senior coalition partner royalist troops have been pushed back to remote areas of northern Cambodia in clashes with Hun Sen's troops.

Government forces under Hun Sen took full control of the key northwestern border town of Poipet after Ranariddh's men either defected to Hun Sen's side or withdrew to join their comrades in the forest, officials in the town said on Thursday.

The town, the main trading point on Cambodia's border with Thailand, has been tense since Ranariddh's ouster on July 6 and a brief clash between the rival forces on Sunday left four soldiers dead and eight wounded.
